papers.title: De Novo-Designed Alpha-Helical Proteins Enable Ligand-Directed Spectral Tuning
papers.abstract: Canonical green fluorescent proteins typically regulate chromophore photophysics through a rigid beta-barrel environment, while spectral tuning often relies on protein engineering or directed evolution. Here, we design a compact alpha-helical protein pocket that activates a GFP-chromophore-derived fluorogen and accommodates a series of chemically modified ligands. A co-crystal structure reveals shared anchoring interactions for fluorogen activation and contacts that enable ligand-dependent spectral tuning. Guided by this structure, ligand substitution shifts emission across the red-to-green range while retaining the same protein scaffold. Quantitative binding and photophysical analyses establish the structural and chemical determinants of affinity, fluorescence activation, and spectral tuning, and the resulting fluorogens function in living cells. Finally, structure-guided substitutions repurpose the pocket toward a distinct drug ligand. These results establish an alpha-helical route to programmable fluorogen activation in which optical properties can be tuned through ligand design rather than repeated protein evolution.

papers.title: Elucidating the membrane-binding mechanism of the ALPS-like motif of the Osh4 protein
papers.abstract: Transport of lipids within cells is crucial for cellular functions and is facilitated by lipid transport proteins, like the Saccharomyces cerevisiae oxysterol-binding homologue (Osh) proteins. Among these, Osh4 is of particular interest, due to its role in lipid trafficking at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and trans-Golgi network (TGN). Here, we elucidate the membrane-binding mechanism of the amphipathic lipid packing sensor (ALPS)-like motif of Osh4 using circular dichroism, fluorescence spectroscopy, isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) integrated with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Our findings show environment-dependent structural changes of the ALPS peptide, including a preference for -helical structure in the presence of phospholipid membranes which is modestly enhanced in the presence of anionic lipids. Fluorescence spectroscopy and MD simulation results corroborate the ALPS peptide's interaction with model membranes and reveal slightly enhanced binding to membranes containing anionic lipids. Moreover, XRD demonstrated the peptide influences membrane structure, with thinning observed upon peptide incorporation. We determined the binding affinity of the ALPS peptide to model membranes using ITC, which supports enthalpy-driven contributions between anionic lipids and the lysine in the ALPS peptide and an entropic contribution from serine and threonine residues desolvating into the membrane. Comparison with computational estimates using potential of mean force calculations suggests current force fields overestimate binding energy. Overall, our results support that the ALPS-like motif will preferentially bind to the TGN cytosolic leaflet, which contains a higher concentration of anionic lipids compared to the ER, providing insight into lipid transport by Osh4.

papers.title: Predicting the antigenic peptidome
papers.abstract: Antigenic peptides are short protein sequences that are recognized by the immune system. The Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) transports intracellular peptides to the cell surface, where interactions with CD8+ T cells are induced. Peptide presentation involves a complex transport pathway, which has several key checkpoints and involves kinetic proofreading. Here, we show that cell metabolism, by modulating transport checkpoints, can strongly affect antigen presentation. We predict the presentation of individual peptides from peptide-specific data - intracellular concentration and MHC binding affinity - and the transmission characteristics of the transport pathway. Together, these factors determine the total amount and the specific distribution of peptides available for T-cell recognition, depending on the metabolic state of the cell. We validate the underlying model by combining RNA-seq expression data, inferred MHC-binding constants, and mass spectrometry data for peptides presented across different cell lines. We map characteristic shifts in the presented peptidome between healthy and cancer cell lines and infer underlying changes in transport checkpoints, including variations in peptide supply and MHC expression. Together, the model establishes a predictive link between immunogenicity and the metabolic landscape of the presenting cell.

papers.title: The C-tail governs isoform-specific local and global conformational dynamics of non-visual arrestins in aqueous and membrane environments
papers.abstract: Non-visual arrestins, {beta}-arrestin 1 ({beta}-arr1) and {beta}-arrestin 2 ({beta}-arr2), regulate GPCR desensitization, internalization, and signaling, making them potentially attractive therapeutic targets in several diseases. However, their high sequence similarity complicates isoform- specific targeting. Their C-tails exhibit considerably lower sequence conservation, but they remain poorly characterized due to their disordered nature, limiting our understanding of how C-tail conformational dynamics influence arrestin structure and function. To address this gap, we investigated how C-tail dynamics shape conformational landscape of non-visual arrestins and their membrane interactions using millisecond-scale coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. Our findings reveal isoform-specific contributions of the arrestin core and C-tail to activation- related motifs, interdomain rotation, and intramolecular communication networks. Notably, C- tail-swapped constructs largely recapitulated the conformational behavior associated with the corresponding C-tail isoform, highlighting the transferable nature of C-tail-encoded dynamic properties. The isoforms also displayed distinct membrane-binding modes: {beta}-arr1 preferentially engaged the membrane through C-domain, whereas {beta}-arr2 used N-domain. C- tail truncation further altered membrane-binding mode of {beta}-arr1, underscoring the regulatory role of the distal tail in membrane engagement. In addition to wild-type proteins, we examined the effects of disease-associated mutations on the C-tail dynamics. {beta}-arr1T224N and {beta}-arr2T268I mutants, reported to co-occur in a lung cancer patient sample in the COSMIC database, induced distinct conformational profiles where the former displayed inactive-like whereas the latter favored active-like dynamics. Overall, our findings highlight C-tail dynamics as a key determinant of isoform-specific arrestin regulation and suggest that disease-associated mutations may reshape arrestin conformational landscapes, potentially affecting their function. These insights may guide the development of isoform- and mutation-specific therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Molecular mechanisms driving the Arctic E22G-induced amyloidogenicity switch between Aβ40 and Aβ42
papers.abstract: Amyloid fibrils formed by amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) are characterized by parallel in-register (PAIR) interpeptide {beta}-sheets. Although A{beta}42 is more amyloidogenic than the more abundant A{beta}40 isoform, the familial Arctic E22G mutation disproportionately enhances the amyloidogenicity of A{beta}40, effectively reversing this relationship. To uncover the molecular mechanisms underlying this differential response, we systematically compared the monomeric conformational ensembles and dimerization dynamics of both wild-type (WT) and E22G mutant A{beta}40 and A{beta}42 using long-timescale atomistic discrete molecular dynamics simulations with enhanced sampling by replica permutation. We found that the propensity to form extended inter-peptide PAIR alignments in dimerization recapitulates the relative amyloidogenicity of the four A{beta} variants. Our results reveal an isoform-dependent balance between electrostatic frustration near residues 22-23 and the stabilizing interactions gained upon productive PAIR assembly. In WT A{beta}42, the two additional C-terminal residues promote formation of an extended conformation spanning the central hydrophobic core (CHC) and adjacent sequence. Upon PAIR alignment, the resulting backbone hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts provide sufficient stabilization to compensate for unfavorable electrostatic interactions involving E22 and D23. In contrast, A{beta}40 forms shorter {beta}-strands within CHC and more frequently adopts off-register parallel or antiparallel intermolecular {beta}-sheets, making electrostatic frustration a greater barrier towards productive PAIR assembly. Neutralization of E22 by the Arctic E22G mutation therefore lowers this barrier more strongly in A{beta}40 than in A{beta}42, providing a molecular explanation for the mutation-induced reversal of their relative amyloidogenicity. Together, these results establish an isoform-dependent mechanism by which {beta}-strand preorganization modulates the impact of electrostatic frustration on early A{beta} assembly and support PAIR alignment as a structural reaction coordinate for characterizing fibril-nucleating interactions.

papers.title: Structure-Guided Design of a c-Src-Inspired Polypeptide Inhibitor Targeting KRas4B-G12D
papers.abstract: Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (KRas) is among the most frequently mutated oncogenes in human cancers, so that its direct inhibition remains a major therapeutic challenge. Here, we present a comprehensive computational investigation of a 41-residue chimeric polypeptide proposed as a potential binder of KRas4B-G12D. Our approach integrates conventional and enhanced sampling techniques, molecular docking, extensive molecular dynamics simulations, binding free-energy calculations, and per-residue energy decomposition analysis, amounting to a cumulative simulation time of 35.6 microseconds. Our work revealed that the primary state of the polypeptide (State A) consistently preferred KRas4B-G12D over the wild-type counterpart, irrespective of the nucleotide state. Structural and energetic analyses indicate that this selectivity of polypeptide arises mainly from interactions between its N-terminal region (residues 1-23) and the KRas switch regions, rather than direct contact with residue 12. These findings support an indirect ensemble-mediated recognition mechanism, in which mutation-induced shifts in the KRas conformational landscape modulate polypeptide binding. By revealing how a compact chimeric polypeptide can discriminate a single-residue oncogenic mutation through conformational recognition, this work establishes a benchmark for a new generation of mutant-selective peptide therapeutics, with the potential to transform the current strategies for the design of drugs targeting KRas mutations which are among the deadliest and least treatable in oncology.

papers.title: Clustering conformations from molecular dynamics simulations by gradient flow segmentation of projected free energy landscapes
papers.abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations sample a continuum of conformations whose populations can reveal distinct protein structural states and substates as well as different ligand binding states. Determining which conformations belong to each state remains a central challenge in interpreting protein structural dynamics and ligand binding. Building on our framework for constructing free-energy surfaces from principal component projections of MD trajectories, we treat these surfaces as images. We adapt a method originally developed to segment cell nuclei in three-dimensional microscopy images and use the basin structure of the free-energy surface as the basis for clustering. We follow gradient flow toward free-energy minima and group neighboring regions by comparing the free energy along their shared boundaries with that within each region. When both regions contain resolved minima, we also test how far apart their cores are relative to their internal variation. Mapping the regions associated with the minima back to the original trajectories recovers the conformational ensemble in each state or substate and allows us to select a representative conformation directly from the simulation. We applied the method to conformational changes in the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein and the leucine transporter LeuT, and to the binding conformations sampled by a small-molecule drug interacting with the PP2A scaffold PR65. By combining statistical mechanics with computer vision, this approach provides a structural interpretation of how sampled conformational populations are organized

papers.title: MembraneCurvature: A Python tool to calculate membrane curvature from molecular dynamics simulations.
papers.abstract: Biological membranes are complex structural and functional assemblies that play central roles in many cellular processes. They are primarily composed of lipids and proteins, whose dynamics and interactions are commonly investigated at the molecular level using Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations. Local membrane curvature, arising from changes in lipid composition and lipid-protein interactions, is an important property linked to lipid and protein sorting as well as protein mechanisms of action. Here, we present MembraneCurvature, a fast, user-friendly, and fully documented Python package designed to compute membrane curvature from MD simulations. Using selected lipid atoms as a reference, MembraneCurvature derives membrane surfaces and calculates molecular descriptors such as mean and Gaussian curvature. The package is built on top of the MDAnalysis library, a versatile framework compatible with simulations obtained from different software, force fields and membranes of simple or complex compositions. To demonstrate its application, we analyze MD simulations of a model plasma membrane generated using the Martini force field, both in the presence and absence of the phospholipid efflux ABC transporter ABCA1. In this example, MembraneCurvature identifies persistent, protein-induced membrane curvature that depends on the protein's conformational state and that is leaflet-specific.

papers.title: Fundamental limits on fluorescence lifetime estimation using optical gating
papers.abstract: Fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM) is a promising approach for quantitative measurement in biology. Traditional lifetime measurements have limited photon throughput and slow acquisition speed due to photon counting electronics and point-scanning detectors. Wide-field imaging with optical gating can overcome these limitations. We analyze lifetime estimation precision for both single- and bi-exponential decays with optical gating waveforms. We focus on electro-optic (EO-FLIM) gating approaches that can be implemented all-optically with no photon loss and compare them to standard binning methods. Fisher information (FI) is used to calculate the Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) for decay parameter estimation for each gating strategy, which is then verified with maximum likelihood estimation on Monte Carlo simulated data. We present fundamental limits for both single and bi-exponential estimation with resonant, step, and square gating waveforms. For single exponential decays, a single step or resonant gate approaches the FI limits from time correlated single photon counting (TC-SPC) within a factor of 1.2-1.6x. We map the parameter space for laser excitation waveform, gate waveform, and gate number. For bi-exponential estimation, at least 3 parallel step or resonant gates are required to estimate the full parameters. With prior knowledge of one lifetime, two optimally-chosen gates can approach the TC-SPC limit within 1.6x (step gate) or 2.9x (resonant gate). Estimation precision converges within 5-10 gates across conditions with one known lifetime component and within 10-15 gates with no prior information. Asymptotic performance with increasing gate number achieves between 3.1x (step) and 3.7x (resonant) the TC-SPC limit with one known lifetime and between 3.5x (step) and 8.8x (resonant) with no prior information. These results inform the design of sparse gating strategies that maximize throughput and per-photon information for lifetime estimation. Optical gating enables future experiments for high-throughput sensing and multiplexing of fluorescent biosensors without relying on time-resolved detector electronics.

papers.title: A single LIM domain is sufficient for strain-selective binding of zyxin to F-actin
papers.abstract: Cells sense mechanical cues through force-dependent changes in protein binding and activity, and the actin cytoskeleton is a central conduit for these forces. Zyxin and other LIM (Lin-11, Isl-1, Mec-3) domain proteins accumulate on strained F-actin through their LIM containing region (LCR), a process we term strain-selective binding. In cells, zyxin's LCR, which contains three tandem LIM domains, is necessary and sufficient for its force-dependent actin cytoskeleton localization, but the minimal unit required for strain-selective binding, in both the number of zyxin molecules and the number of LIM domains, is unknown. Here, we use an in vitro contractile network assay and multi-color TIRF microscopy to quantify the binding of full-length zyxin and LCR truncations to actomyosin bundles. Myosin II-dependent perturbations of F-actin bundles increase zyxin binding ~14-fold. Zyxin binds as clusters of 2-3 molecules with a median lifetime of ~80 s, independent of the number of molecules per cluster. The zyxin binding density is also independent of the number of actin filaments in a bundle. Each of zyxin's three LIM domains alone is sufficient for myosin-dependent binding, with binding density and lifetime similar to those of full length zyxin. The LIM domains differ in their tendency to cluster, which structure predictions suggest arises from hydrophobic LIM-LIM interfaces. Together, these data show that a single LIM domain is the minimal unit required for strain-selective binding of zyxin to F-actin. Zyxin binds rare, myosin-generated sites on actin filaments as clusters of 2-3 molecules, but neither clustering nor tandem LIM domains are required for this binding in vitro.

papers.title: Length and Mg2+ dependent conformational changes in homopolymeric single-stranded RNA sequences
papers.abstract: Despite the important functional roles of single-stranded RNA molecules in a number of biological processes, relatively little is known about their conformational ensemble, especially in divalent cations. We use the coarse-grained Three Interaction Site model for RNA (TIS-RNA) to determine the structural changes in rA30, rA120, and rU30 as a function of Mg2+ concentration at a fixed monovalent concentration. The Mg2+-dependent excess ions around rA30 and rU30, obtained in simulations, are in good agreement with experiments. Importantly, the agreement between the simulated structure factor and measurements using small angle X-ray scattering is excellent both in the absence and presence of Mg2+. rA30 retains local helical order across the Mg2+ concentrations studied, including 0 mM, whereas rU30 remains disordered. The simulations lead to two predictions. (1) Both rA30 and rA120 populate two distinct states (one more compact than the other) as the Mg2+ concentration is increased. At high Mg2+ concentrations (30 mM), only the compact state survives in rA120, whereas in rA30 the extended and compact states coexist. (2) The compact states of both rA30 and rA120 are hairpin-like and are stabilized by non-neighboring stacking interactions. Such stacks are common in folded RNA structures, and we derived the associated parameters by analyzing more than 2,600 PDB structures. The predictions may be tested using single-molecule Forster resonance energy transfer (smFRET) experiments. Plausible implications of the results for Mg2+-induced phase separation are briefly outlined.

papers.title: Space partitioning by microtubules and molecular motors
papers.abstract: Cells contain radial arrays or polar bundles of microtubules that support their main functions. Active matter made of microtubules and molecular motors can transiently assemble radial asters or form nematic structures that continuously extend and fold. Whether such networks can reach dynamic steady states, as seen in cells, is not known. Here we asked whether confining two oppositely directed motors could generate dynamic, stable and regular organizations. Microtubules alignment and polarity sorting formed linear stacks that partitioned the available space into domains enriched in one motor or the other. Motor ratio, microtubule number and length, and the size and shape of the confinement determined whether the resulting domain organizations were radial, polar, bipolar or multipolar. Similar patterns formed in living cells upon microtubule stabilization. These findings reveal regular, dynamic steady-states in confined active matter and open new ways to understand the diversity of microtubule network architectures in cells.

papers.title: ProFORGE: a composable sequence structure dynamics workflow validated by mechanoprotein design
papers.abstract: Designing a protein to resist tension requires identifying the contacts that bear the load. We developed ProFORGE to track residues as a scaffold changes length and to select designs by steered molecular dynamics. Starting with the 56-residue GB1 domain, we generated 14,542 candidates using protein language models for scaffold expansion and fixed-backbone design for sequence refinement. Of 182 sequences that passed the initial screen in the final round, 19 also met the AlphaFold 3 confidence threshold. The number of backbone hydrogen bonds between the terminal strands correlated with mean peak force at both simulated pulling speeds (Spearman ensuremath{rho} = 0.83--0.85). Two 98-residue designs shared less than 10% global sequence identity with wild-type GB1. In single-molecule magnetic-tweezers measurements, their most probable unfolding forces were 117.9 and 132.1~pN, or 5.5 and 5.8 times those of the wild-type domains measured on the same tethers.

papers.title: Brillouin microscopy detects treatment-associated biophysical responses in live triple-negative breast cancer spheroids
papers.abstract: Mechanical changes are increasingly recognised as an integral component of tumour response to therapy and can be effectively used as a tumour biomarker in designing and testing new anticancer therapies. Assessing these changes in situ in a live tumour model, however, without disturbing cellular function, remains a challenge. We investigated dose-dependent responses to anticancer drugs in live three-dimensional triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) spheroids using label-free Brillouin microscopy, complemented by bulk compression testing and biological assays. Increasing drug concentration produced a progressive reduction in apparent stiffness of the tumour spheroids, accompanied by a reduction in Brillouin frequency shift, indicating treatment-associated mechanical softening of spheroids. These mechanical responses were accompanied by drug-dependent changes in cell cycle-associated signals and membrane-integrity markers. Spatially resolved Brillouin mapping revealed the heterogeneous distribution of spheroid mechanical properties. The combined approach based on bulk spheroid compression and microscale Brillouin mapping provides an integrated dual-scale view of treatment-associated mechanics in live tumour models. Importantly, Brillouin microscopy detected spectral changes in conditions where the relative metabolic activity of intact spheroids remained statistically unchanged. Together, these findings highlight the potential of Brillouin microscopy for detecting early responses to anticancer drugs, supporting a greater focus on individualised approaches to monitoring tumour response.

papers.title: Bonds, a neighbourhood field and missing hydrogens: a transferable electron-density model of proteins
papers.abstract: A compound that has not been made has no diffraction data to refine against. A model of electron density that is to be used in drug design must therefore be transferable: the same numbers for every protein and every ligand, nothing fitted per structure. The independent-atom model (IAM) is transferable, but it places no density in bonds and lets no atom respond to its surroundings. We set out to add both, explicitly and with few parameters, and tested each step on every Protein Data Bank X-ray entry with structure factors at 1.0 Angstrom or better (2,006 entries; 650 proteins never seen in training). Four things were learnt on the way. The benchmark itself had to be corrected first: in models deposited without hydrogen atoms, placing riding hydrogens lowers the R of the IAM by 0.0093 in 315 of 316 proteins, and about four fifths of what a transferable multipole model appeared to gain on them was the missing hydrogens. With hydrogens placed on every model, a layer that names each bond and contact, gives it one charge and one width and takes that charge from the valence shells of its atoms (the Complete Electron-cloud Layer, CEL) lowers R in 611 of 650 proteins, but by only 0.0007. Most of what the IAM leaves out is centred on the atoms and set by their surroundings. A neighbourhood field of 3,055 parameters, computed by matrix products from the types and distances of all atoms within 8 Angstrom, lowers R three times more than the bond layer, and the two together (3,214 parameters) are better than the multipole (4,768) in 545 of 650 proteins. And a bond has to be named by its chemical environment: with one class per pair of elements the C-N bond came out negative; with 25 classes defined beforehand the peptide bond is positive, the carbon skeleton carries 0.04 to 0.12 electrons per bond in a chemical order, and the layer is better on 602 of 650 unseen proteins. Read inversely, the bonds of the main chain stand out of the density in more than four proteins of five, and the polar bonds of ligands, which read below empty points in the density left by independent atoms, are restored by the field predicted from the surroundings, with its factor calibrated on ligand bonds against the per-atom solution. A per-atom solution of the same radial form lowers R by 0.017 on the reflections it is fitted to, but by about 0.002 on reflections held out of the fit, which is the size of what the field predicted from distances already delivers: the spherical form is close to what the data support, and the next gain has to come from direction. The bonds respond to their surroundings as well, but as a secondary effect: freed bond by bond and tested on held-out reflections, the charge of a bond changes by about 0.06 electron and gives one tenth of the gain of the atoms, and no shift of the bond charge is supported by the data.

papers.title: Escherichia coli siphovirus DH23 features unusual C12-C13-C6 symmetry of the neck complex and the lateral tail fibers branching from the central tail fiber
papers.abstract: Bacteriophages capable of propagating in host cells that have entered or are approaching the early stationary phase of growth (eSPI phages) are promising candidates for phage therapy as they may efficiently destroy slowly growing pathogen populations in vivo. Among the Escherichia coli phages, the eSPI phenotype is rare and the diversity of such phages is limited. Siphoviruses of the Dhillonvirus genus appear to offer an attractive platform for implementing host range management systems. We investigated the structure of the eSPI Dhillonvirus DH23 using cryo-electron microscopy and single-particle analysis and revealed that its adaptor protein connecting the dodecameric head portal to the hexamer ring of the tail termination protein forms a tridecameric (C13) ring rather than a dodecameric ring as in most known bacteriophages. Despite the presence of the putative lateral tail fiber (LTF) protein gene in the DH23 genome, the tail tip 3D density map showed no evidence of LTF attachment. Examination of 2D projection images of the flexible distal part of the central tail fiber (CTF) revealed a massive density from which the LTFs emanate, forming a branched CTF-LTF structure that was not seen in coliphages previously.

papers.title: Segmental Acceleration in Protein Condensates
papers.abstract: Biomolecular condensates are essential to cellular processes and organization, and are typically formed by weak, multivalent interactions among biomolecules, such as intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). Because condensates are much more viscous than the surrounding solution, they are generally expected to slow protein motions. While the length-scale-dependent dynamics of IDPs in dilute and dense phases have been studied separately, a systematic comparison of how these dynamics change upon phase separation remains lacking. In this study, we use coarse-grained, explicit-solvent molecular dynamics simulations to compare the segmental dynamics between the dilute and dense phases of the low-complexity domain of the RNA-binding protein Fused in Sarcoma (FUS-LC) and compositionally similar model IDPs of different lengths. Short protein segments, contrary to expectation, relax faster within the condensate than in the dilute phase, whereas segments longer than about one-seventh of the chain relax more slowly. Our results suggest that this crossover arises because chain collapse in the dilute phase slows local relaxation, whereas neighboring chains in the condensate slow chain-scale relaxation. The dilute phase sets both the magnitude of the speed-up and the segment length up to which it extends: dilute-phase relaxation changes with chain length and interaction strength, whereas relaxation within the condensate, at a fixed protein concentration, does not. Slower water dynamics increase the speed-up, whereas removing water eliminates it. Overall, our results suggest that condensates slow global protein motions but accelerate local ones, which may help preserve the liquid-like nature of the condensate's interior.

papers.title: Modeling three-dimensional structures of flaviviral exoribonuclease-resistant RNAs by combining functional and computational analyses
papers.abstract: Exoribonuclease-resistant RNAs (xrRNAs) are non-coding RNAs used by viruses to evade host RNase-mediated degradation. In flaviviruses, xrRNAs are thought to share an unusual knot-like fold with the 5'-end threaded through a ring formed by a multi-helix junction and closed by a pseudoknot, but only a handful of high-resolution structures have been solved to date. We combined structure prediction tools with mutational analysis of RNase resistance to determine previously unsolved 3D structures of xrRNAs from the West Nile virus (WNV) and two dengue virus (DENV) serotypes. We first predicted possible pseudoknot structures computationally, then tested them by systematically mutating putatively pseudoknotted bases and assessing RNase resistance to discriminate between models. The successful pseudoknot models were used to predict 3D structures computationally, refining the models by identifying tertiary contacts at the threaded 5' end via another round of mutagenesis and RNase resistance testing. We found that all 3 xrRNAs shared the same threaded knot-like architecture as in experimentally solved flaviviral xrRNAs, with similar tertiary contacts generating an analogous hierarchy of interactions importance for RNase resistance, but the pseudoknot length varied considerably, from 8 pairs in WNV to 2 in DENV2. This work illustrates a powerful new approach for determining xrRNA structures that are hard to obtain by high-resolution experimental methods by integrating computational predictions with functional assays.

papers.title: Protein docking on DNA surfaces using de novo designed binders
papers.abstract: Positioning proteins on DNA-functionalized surfaces offers a way to organize catalytic, recognition and signaling activities across materials from synthetic particles to programmable nanostructures. However, site-specific attachment typically requires protein-oligonucleotide conjugation. Here we adapt a small, de novo designed protein that binds a six-base-pair sequence from one duplex face into a genetically encoded surface adapter. We define geometric constraints near blunt ends, hairpin loops and crossover junctions, and identify linker and site-spacing combinations that increase tandem cis-dimer affinity. In synthetic macrophage receptors, these dimers trigger phagocytosis of DNA-coated beads, preserve sensitivity to origami ligand spacing, and remain active after a 24-hour delay when DNA-conjugated receptors decline. We also design trans-dimers bridging neighboring origami helices to dock fluorescent proteins, enzymes, an antibody fragment and SpyCatcher cargo. Together, these design rules and binding modes establish a modular framework for genetically encoded protein-DNA interfacing that should generalize to new de novo binders.

papers.title: Molpylot: a shared workspace for human-AI collaboration in molecular simulation
papers.abstract: Rigorous biomolecular simulation requires a long chain of physical decisions across fragmented tools. Language-model agents offer to automate this work, yet current agents operate outside the scientist's environment, generating ad hoc scripts or files that are effortless to launch but laborious to inspect and verify. Here we introduce Molpylot, an interactive modeling platform that unifies structure preparation, molecular dynamics, specialist protocols and replica-aware analysis in a graphical workspace designed to be immediate for the scientist, while exposing that same live session to any language model through 256 typed, tested tools. Operating within this shared workspace, the agent executes routine tasks under built-in safeguards that catch physical inconsistencies, while scientific judgment stays with the scientist. Across 18 systems, including asymmetric membranes, quantum-parameterized metal sites, enhanced sampling and free-energy calculations, we show how agents and built-in checks streamline setup, quality control and trajectory analysis. Molpylot is free for noncommercial use.

papers.title: Transcriptional activation forms insulation boundaries through cohesin-independent decompaction and cohesin-dependent barrier formation
papers.abstract: How 3D genome structure regulates transcription has been intensely studied, but how transcription regulates 3D genome structure remains poorly understood. To elucidate this relationship, we integrate Region Capture Micro-C and simultaneous live-cell imaging of CTCF chromatin looping and inducible nascent transcription at the Fbn2 locus with 3D polymer modeling and perturbation experiments. We find that transcription activation induces cohesin-independent insulation boundary formation at the Fbn2 promoter, locus decompaction, and faster chromatin dynamics. We also show that transcriptional bursts interfere with CTCF loop formation in living cells. Using 3D polymer modeling to distinguish plausible mechanistic models, we find that transcription-induced gene body decompaction can explain increased mobility and cohesin-independent insulation, while a polymerase-associated barrier to loop extrusion can explain transcription-linked looping changes. Together, these results reveal cohesin-dependent and -independent mechanisms through which transcription can establish insulation and regulate 3D genome structure.

papers.title: Structural deformations of lipid bilayers around membrane proteins inform oligomerization type
papers.abstract: A functional definition of a membrane protein's structure is the three-dimensional arrangement of the polypeptide and the structure of the membrane around it. Biological membranes are composed of self-assembled lipid bilayers, with membrane proteins acting as inclusions that perturb this phase. These inclusions induce long-range changes in membrane structure and create an intrinsic, lipid-mediated driving force for membrane protein association. The question is how much different membrane protein folds shape their surrounding membrane to tune the affinity and specificity of this driving force. To investigate this, we conducted a computational study to evaluate whether different membrane protein oligomers exhibit characteristic membrane defects that indicate specificity in complexation. We performed coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of monomeric and oligomeric states of ten different channels and transporters in POPC bilayers and evaluated changes in membrane thickness, deformation energy, and lipid packing parameters. We found that all the proteins affect their surrounding membrane up to 3 nm from the protein surface. However, we observed larger defects at oligomeric interfaces for obligatory or structurally monomorphic complexes, suggesting that their oligomerization is partly driven by burial of membrane defects. In contrast, oligomers that adopt different quaternary structures across homologs show weaker perturbations at known binding interfaces, and larger perturbations at lipid-facing surfaces. Nevertheless, all systems show fewer membrane defects upon oligomerization, suggesting an underlying lipid-mediated driving force that each protein fold modulates to tune affinity via membrane-mediated oligomerization.

papers.title: Near-surface flight enhances thrust in an insect-inspired flapping-wing robot
papers.abstract: A number of semi-aquatic insects rapidly move across the water surface using interfacial flight. In this locomotion strategy, flapping wings generate thrust above the air-water interface while surface tension supports their weight. This close proximity to the air-water interface alters aerodynamic force generation through ground effect, potentially enhancing horizontal propulsion. Here, we demonstrate that near-surface flapping enhances horizontal thrust by up to 17% at shallow stroke-plane inclinations. Using a beetle-inspired flapping-wing robot, we systematically vary wing-surface distance (D/c, where D is the minimum trailing-edge-to-surface clearance during flapping, normalised by chord length c) and stroke plane inclination {beta} at Reynolds numbers of order 103. Locomotion experiments show increased acceleration and higher terminal velocity near the surface (D/c < 1) at shallow stroke plane angles ({beta} = 30{degrees} and 45{degrees}), while direct wind-tunnel force measurements confirm increased aerodynamic thrust, distinguishing this enhancement from changes in water-related resistance. Particle image velocimetry further reveals that near-surface flapping alters passive wing motion and surrounding flow, producing stronger backward-directed flow after stroke reversal and earlier leading-edge vortex development during the initial upstroke. These findings establish a configuration-dependent aerodynamic benefit of near-surface flapping, providing insight into insect-scale interfacial flight and opportunities for enhancing propulsion in bio-inspired robotic systems.

papers.title: Insights into Ice-Growth Inhibition and Hydration Ordering by the Ca2+-Dependent Antifreeze Protein MaIBP_RIV
papers.abstract: Antifreeze proteins (AFPs) inhibit ice growth by binding to specific ice surfaces, although the molecular basis of this activity remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate the ice-growth inhibition mechanism of the calcium-dependent antifreeze protein MaIBP_RIV from Marinomonas arctica using all-atom molecular dynamics simulations. MaIBP_RIV exhibits stable binding to the primary prism and basal ice planes through its ice-binding surface (IBS), effectively suppressing ice growth. IBS binding to the secondary prism plane is weaker and only temporarily inhibits growth. In contrast, the non-ice-binding surface (non-IBS) is repelled by the growing ice front. Our results also explain that Ca2+; stabilises the IBS and essential for ice-growth inhibition, while removing Ca2+; reduces IBS flatness, which significantly impairs its ice-growth activity. Experimentally characterised mutations on IBS residues (S44Y, G63D, N65Y, and D87Y) result in continuous ice growth, consistent with their reduced antifreeze activity. Hydration analysis of water molecules around IBS and non-IBS suggests that, by decreasing the temperature from 300K to 240K, the water molecules around IBS show more ice-like ordering compared to those around the non-IBS.

papers.title: Isolating soluble, near-native, misfolded states and their functional characterization: A step towards high-resolution protein misfolding structures
papers.abstract: Proteins can misfold into soluble, near-native states that act as long-lived kinetic traps with aggregation independent biological consequences. A key step toward obtaining high-resolution structures of these states is the ability to isolate/purify them. Here, we show this is possible for the Escherichia coli protein pyruvate kinase (pykF) following refolding from chemical denaturant. After controlling for aggregates the refolded (treatment) ensemble exhibits a decrease in average specific activity relative to the untreated (natively folded) sample. Size exclusion chromatography reveals two distinct populations in this treatment group, whereas the untreated group exhibits a single population. Native PAGE analysis finds that both populations from the treatment group have the same mass and electrophoretic mobility as the untreated protein, consistent with native-like global properties and oligomerization state. Functional analysis using Michaelis-Menten kinetics shows that one population retains activity comparable to the untreated sample, while the other has no detectable activity, indicating that approximately 31 +/- 17.9% (95% Confidence Interval) of refolded molecules are soluble, near-native, but non-functional. ANS fluorescence measurements probing hydrophobic surface exposure further show that the non-functional population has altered surface properties relative to the active population. Differences in these properties persist for at least four hours following renaturation, indicating the system remains out-of-equilibrium. Together, these results demonstrate that size exclusion chromatography can be used to isolate soluble, non-aggregating, misfolded states that are structurally similar to the native state yet functionally inactive. This approach provides a basis for enriching such misfolded states for subsequent high-resolution structural characterization.

papers.title: VMDance: An Efficient and Interactive Molecular Dynamics Clustering Plugin for VMD
papers.abstract: Clustering is the standard route from a molecular dynamics trajectory to a small set of interpretable conformational states, yet it is usually performed outside the molecular viewer, leaving cluster assignments to be exported, tracked, and mapped back onto the structures by hand. We present VMDance, an open-source plugin that brings the MDANCE family of $n$-ary similarity clustering methods into VMD. Through a graphical interface backed by a C++ implementation, it provides kmeans{} NANI, HELM, eQual, and DIVINE clustering, together with PRIME representative-structure selection. These methods scale linearly with the number of frames and support deterministic initialization, so partitions can be reproduced exactly and recomputed interactively. Cluster assignments, quality metrics, and representative structures are linked to the loaded trajectory, keeping the analysis of conformational states alongside the structures themselves. VMDance is freely available at url{https://github.com/diegoenry/vmd-mdance-plugin}

papers.title: Beyond the Classical Flake-to-Vesicle Mechanism: Non-standard Vesicles Arise from S-Shaped Intermediates
papers.abstract: Vesicles are indispensable tools across numerous scientific and pharmaceutical fields, however, optimizing their properties necessitates a comprehensive understanding of their formation mechanism. The formation of lipid vesicles from bilayered lipid flakes has long been recognized as a fundamental step in vesicle preparation. The classical flake-to-vesicle mechanism, grounded in continuum models, describes this process as the transformation of a lipid flake into a regular spherical vesicle (RSV) via a cup-shaped intermediate. Nevertheless, this classical mechanism fails to account for emerging experimental observations of non-standard vesicles exhibiting diverse morphologies. Here, using extensive coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations combined with Markov state model analysis, we systematically revisit this transition process at near-atomic resolution. In addition to the standard product, we observe a notable fraction of non-standard vesicles, including small-sized spherical vesicles (SSVs), ellipsoidal vesicles (ELVs), and flake-derived vesicle complexes (FVCs). These non-standard products arise from S-shaped intermediates that differ from the classical cup-shaped intermediate, and the degree of S-shapedness is closely correlated with whether non-standard vesicles are generated and, if so, which specific types. This correlation holds consistently across four lipid systems with distinct compositions and transbilayer distributions. On this basis, we propose a generalized mechanism that explicitly incorporates the S-shaped intermediates and the non-standard vesicles. This new mechanism opens new opportunities for the innovative development of engineered vesicles with tailored morphologies for diagnostics, drug delivery, and therapeutics.

papers.title: Integrating hydrogen-exchange experiments with conformational ensembles
papers.abstract: Protein conformational dynamics are central to biological function but remain difficult to characterise at scale. Amide hydrogen exchange (HX), measured by NMR or mass spectrometry, probes these dynamics but requires computational models for integration with structural ensembles. We benchmark models for calculating HX from ensembles using a large literature-derived dataset spanning folded and intrinsically disordered proteins. We then develop a model that identifies exchange-competent amides from local structural descriptors while accounting for electrostatic effects. The model predicts protection across a broad dynamic range in ensembles generated by molecular dynamics and generative AI. HX-guided ensemble reweighting improves agreement with independent NMR, SAXS, and folding-stability measurements. Millisecond HX distinguishes and refines alternative ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins, while reweighting of structured proteins reveals folding intermediates and low-population excited states. These results establish HX as a quantitative restraint for ensemble reweighting and provide a scalable framework for benchmarking simulations and generative protein models.

papers.title: From Growth Inhibition to Fluctuations: Testing an Ising Model of Bacterial Responses to Antibiotics
papers.abstract: Complex networks of biochemical reactions have been proposed to exhibit emergent cooperativity that can be described by an effective Ising model, with a small number of parameters encoding collective interactions. Here this mapping is experimentally tested using the response of three bacterial species to a range of antibiotics acting on different cellular targets. The Ising description is compared to the conventional Hill model, examining both the mean growth-rate response and, importantly, its population growth-rate heterogeneity (PGRH). While both models describe the mean growth-rate dependence on antibiotic concentration comparably well, we find that the Ising model provides a markedly better description of PGRH, offering an additional and more stringent test of the collective description. The fitted Ising interaction strength is systematically related to the Hill exponent and increases with the functional distance of the antibiotic target from the protein-production machinery. These results provide experimental support for describing complex biochemical reaction networks through effective cooperative Ising interactions, and suggest that the collective response of bacterial growth to antibiotics reflects the organization of the underlying metabolic network.

papers.title: Automated Transcription Factor Cluster Analysis Toolkit (ATAT)
papers.abstract: Many nuclear regulatory proteins, including transcription factors (TFs) form clusters often referred to as hubs or condensates. These clusters vary widely in their enrichment, size, and persistence, yet tools for quantifying these properties are typically developed for individual datasets. Here, we present the Automated TF Cluster Analysis Toolkit (ATAT), a Python-based toolkit for quantifying TF clustering in four-dimensional fluorescence microscopy data. ATAT combines two analytical pipelines: SCAN, which segments nuclear clusters and measures their spatial distribution, enrichment, and persistence, and LOCK, which quantifies TF enrichment and its dynamics at individual genomic loci. Using live Drosophila embryos, we demonstrate that ATAT distinguishes TF clusters from background fluorescence fluctuations across imaging conditions and resolves differences in TF enrichment and persistence at specific genes. ATAT provides a reproducible framework for investigating the spatial and temporal organization of transcriptional regulators in living cells.
